JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) — On Tuesday, police carrying rubber bullets moved through Johannesburg neighborhoods as authorities tried to stop a recent wave of attacks against foreign nationals. Police said the violence had left 22 people dead and forced an estimated 13,000 others from their homes.

That same day, a mob armed with clubs, machetes and axes rioted on the outskirts of Johannesburg. Many of those targeted were Zimbabweans who had escaped political repression and severe economic hardship in their own country.

Signs of the unrest were visible in one Johannesburg neighborhood, where smoke rose from homes that had been set on fire. Residents angered by the growing number of foreigners coming into South Africa had torched the houses. Firefighters said they had responded to more than 100 fires of that kind since Thursday.

Standing near a line of burned-out homes, Diamond Minnaar said foreigners had only one option. “Most of them just have to go back to their country and leave us in peace,” Minnaar said. “That is the only solution. Or they are just going to get killed. Look at how many shacks have burnt down.”

South African officials and other African leaders have denounced the assaults and looting.

According to police, the violence started a week earlier in Alexandra Township in Johannesburg and has mainly affected the city’s poorest communities.

Dean Christopher Barends, a Lutheran minister in the area, said frustration over poverty and joblessness was helping fuel the unrest. “People are angry because they are unemployed, poverty-affected people struggling for basic needs every day,” he said. “This will explode into something.”

One of the victims, Pascoal Sendela Gulane, a man from Mozambique, said gangs forced their way into his house and took his possessions. He escaped with his family to a church and is now staying with his children in his car on the church grounds. For Gulane and many others, churches and police stations have turned into places of refuge.

On Monday, South African President Thabo Mbeki urged people to stop the attacks. “We dehumanize ourselves the moment we start thinking of another person as less human than we are simply because they come from another country,” he said in a statement. “As South Africans, we must recognize and fully appreciate that we are bound together with other Africans by history, culture, economics and, above all, by destiny. I call upon those behind these shameful and criminal acts to stop! Nothing can justify it.”

Mbeki also requested an investigation into the violence. The same day, the Nelson Mandela Foundation released a statement criticizing what it called “senseless violence.”

Police in South Africa have detained more than 200 people in relation to the unrest, on allegations that include rape, murder, robbery and theft. Police director Govindsamy Mariemuthoo said at least one foreign national had been burned alive over the weekend. Others had their homes set alight, their shops ransacked and their belongings taken.

A CNN producer at the scene reported that police were out in large numbers Tuesday in the neighborhoods where the attacks had happened. Even with officers present, occasional looting continued in several townships east of Johannesburg.

Mbuso Mthembu, the provincial manager of the Red Cross office in Johannesburg, said more people were still fleeing and that the violence appeared to be moving into additional areas. The Red Cross issued an emergency appeal for donations totaling 1 million rand, about $135,000, to assist the roughly 13,000 people who had left their homes.

Mthembu said many people escaped in a hurry and had to abandon everything they owned. “We have delivered blankets, kids clothing, baby formula,” he said. “But we need more.”

The attacks were directed especially at Zimbabweans and other African immigrants, many of whom had settled in South Africa in search of work, safety, and better living conditions.

Violence spread through informal settlements and low-income neighborhoods as crowds burned homes, looted shops, and attacked residents accused of being foreigners. Many migrants fled with only the belongings they could carry, while others sought refuge at police stations, churches, community halls, and temporary shelters. Authorities struggled to contain the unrest as new incidents broke out in different areas, forcing police to use rubber bullets and rapid-response units to disperse mobs and protect threatened communities.

The unrest left 22 people dead and displaced about 13,000 others, creating a humanitarian crisis in and around Johannesburg. Families were separated, homes and businesses were destroyed, and thousands of people were left without food, shelter, or basic security. Aid groups and local organizations worked to provide emergency assistance, while officials appealed for calm and warned that those responsible for the violence would face prosecution.

The attacks drew strong condemnation from South African leaders, as well as from governments and officials across the African continent. They described the violence as unacceptable and damaging to South Africa’s reputation as a country that had once benefited from the support of neighboring African nations during the struggle against apartheid. Community leaders also called for unity and urged residents not to blame migrants for deeper social and economic problems.

The violence highlighted growing tensions in South Africa’s poorest communities, where unemployment, poverty, overcrowding, and poor access to services have fueled resentment and frustration. Many local residents accused foreign migrants of taking jobs, housing, and opportunities, even though analysts and rights groups said the roots of the crisis lay in broader economic inequality and government failures to meet the needs of vulnerable communities.

For many immigrants, particularly Zimbabweans fleeing political and economic hardship at home, South Africa had been seen as a place of refuge. The attacks shattered that sense of safety and exposed how easily economic anger could turn into deadly xenophobic violence. The crisis became a warning of the dangers facing societies where poverty, competition for resources, and hostility toward outsiders are allowed to deepen without effective political and community intervention.

**Johannesburg, South Africa —** A wave of xenophobic violence has swept through parts of Johannesburg, leaving several people dead, dozens injured and thousands of foreign nationals displaced, as police struggled to contain mobs targeting immigrants from elsewhere in Africa.

The unrest, which erupted in townships and informal settlements around the city, has seen shops looted, homes burned and families forced to flee with only the belongings they could carry. Many of those affected are migrants from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, Somalia and other African countries who had settled in South Africa in search of work and safety.

Police said they had deployed additional officers to violence-hit areas and arrested a number of suspects on charges including assault, public violence, arson and robbery. Authorities also said they were working with community leaders to prevent retaliatory attacks and to identify those responsible for inciting the violence.

“We are treating these incidents as serious criminal acts,” a police spokesperson said. “There is no justification for attacks on people because of where they come from.”

Emergency workers reported multiple casualties, while humanitarian groups said shelters and community halls were rapidly filling with displaced foreign nationals. Some victims sought refuge at police stations, churches and temporary camps, fearing further attacks if they returned home.

One Mozambican shopkeeper, standing outside a burned-out storefront, said he had watched years of work disappear in minutes.

“They came shouting that foreigners must leave,” he said. “I ran with my children. We could not save anything.”

A Zimbabwean woman sheltering with her family at a local church said the violence had left her terrified.

“We came here because we thought we would be safe,” she said. “Now we don’t know where to go.”

South Africa has long drawn migrants from across the continent, but high unemployment, poverty and competition for housing and services have fueled tensions in some communities. Rights groups say foreign nationals are often blamed for broader social and economic problems, making them vulnerable to mob violence and political scapegoating.

Former President **Thabo Mbeki** condemned the attacks, warning that xenophobia betrayed South Africa’s own history of struggle against oppression and exile.

“South Africans know what it means to seek refuge and solidarity beyond our borders,” Mbeki said in a statement. “Violence against fellow Africans is a betrayal of the values for which our democracy was founded.”

The **Nelson Mandela Foundation** also denounced the unrest, calling for calm, accountability and renewed efforts to confront prejudice.

“The targeting of people because they are foreign nationals is an attack on human dignity,” the foundation said. “Communities, leaders and institutions must stand together against hatred and protect the vulnerable.”

Local officials said temporary accommodation, food and medical assistance were being arranged for those displaced. But aid workers warned that conditions remained difficult, with many families sleeping on floors and uncertain whether they would be able to return to their homes or businesses.

Community leaders in affected neighborhoods appealed for restraint, saying residents’ frustrations over unemployment and poor services should not be directed at immigrants.

“This is not the solution,” one local organizer said. “Burning homes and attacking people will not create jobs. It only destroys the community.”

Police said patrols would continue in flashpoint areas overnight, while government officials promised further arrests and investigations into organized groups accused of encouraging attacks.

For many of the displaced, however, the immediate concern was survival — and whether the country they had turned to for refuge could still offer them protection.

“We don’t want revenge,” the Zimbabwean mother said. “We just want to live.”

## Anti-foreigner violence leaves dozens dead near Johannesburg

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa —** A wave of anti-foreigner violence that began in townships near Johannesburg has left dozens of people dead, forced tens of thousands from their homes and exposed deep anger over jobs, housing and immigration in post-apartheid South Africa.

The attacks erupted in May 2008 in Alexandra, a densely populated township northeast of Johannesburg, before spreading to other communities in Gauteng province and beyond. Mobs targeted migrants from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, Somalia and other African countries, accusing them of taking jobs, housing and scarce resources.

At least **62 people were killed** in the violence, according to South African authorities and humanitarian groups. Many more were injured, and **tens of thousands were displaced**, seeking safety in police stations, community halls, temporary camps and churches.

In several neighborhoods, witnesses described mobs moving through streets at night, breaking into homes and shops, beating residents and setting shacks alight. Small businesses owned by foreign nationals were looted, their shelves emptied and storefronts burned.

“I ran with only my children and the clothes we were wearing,” said one displaced woman from Zimbabwe sheltering at a church outside Johannesburg. “Everything else is gone — my papers, my blankets, my food. I do not know where we can go now.”

Churches across the region became makeshift shelters, with parish halls and sanctuaries filled with mattresses, donated clothing and families too frightened to return home. Volunteers handed out food and blankets while aid workers warned that overcrowding, cold weather and trauma were worsening the humanitarian crisis.

“We are trying to give people safety first,” said a church volunteer in Johannesburg. “Some have wounds. Some have lost relatives. Many are afraid that if they leave this place, they will be attacked again.”

South African officials condemned the violence and deployed police to affected areas. The government also authorized the military to assist police operations — a rare domestic deployment that underscored the seriousness of the unrest.

Then-President **Thabo Mbeki** denounced the attacks as shameful and said they betrayed South Africa’s history of struggle and solidarity with other African nations. Officials appealed for calm, insisting that criminal behavior and xenophobic violence would not be tolerated.

But in the townships where the attacks began, residents said frustration had been building for years. High unemployment, poverty and a shortage of housing have fueled resentment, especially in informal settlements where South Africans and migrants often live side by side in precarious conditions.

“They say foreigners are the reason we do not have jobs,” said a South African resident in Alexandra. “But the truth is, people here have been poor for a long time. The anger is everywhere, and now people are taking it out on those who are weaker.”

Human rights groups said the violence revealed failures by authorities to address xenophobia and protect vulnerable communities. They also warned that many migrants, particularly Zimbabweans fleeing economic collapse and political turmoil at home, were already living in South Africa with little legal protection or access to services.

For foreign shopkeepers, the destruction was devastating. In one neighborhood, a Somali-owned store was stripped of food, cooking oil and appliances before being set on fire. Nearby residents sifted through the charred remains of homes.

“I worked for years to build that shop,” said one migrant trader. “Now there is nothing. I cannot go back to my country, and I am not safe here.”

Police said arrests were made in connection with killings, assaults, arson and looting, but restoring trust in affected communities remained a challenge. Some displaced people said they would return only if escorted by police; others said they planned to leave South Africa entirely.

Aid agencies urged the government to provide long-term shelter, legal assistance and protection for those displaced, warning that temporary camps and church shelters could not become permanent solutions.

As night fell over Johannesburg’s outskirts, church bells rang over courtyards crowded with families seeking refuge. Inside, children slept under donated blankets while adults quietly discussed whether it would ever be safe to go home.

“We came here because we thought South Africa was a place of hope,” one man from Mozambique said. “Now we are just asking to live.”

**South African Police Struggle to Contain Anti-Immigrant Violence Around Johannesburg**

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa —** South African police deployed reinforcements around Johannesburg as violent mobs continued to target foreigners in a wave of xenophobic attacks that has left communities terrified, displaced thousands of people, and exposed deep frustrations over poverty, unemployment and scarce housing.

The violence, which began in townships near Johannesburg and spread to other parts of the region, has seen crowds armed with sticks, stones and knives attack migrants from other African countries, looting foreign-owned shops and forcing families to flee their homes. Police have used tear gas, rubber bullets and patrols in an effort to disperse mobs and restore order, while dozens of suspects have reportedly been arrested in connection with assaults, arson and theft.

Many of those targeted are immigrants from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, Somalia and other African nations who came to South Africa seeking work, safety or refuge from political and economic hardship. Witnesses described groups moving through informal settlements and poor neighborhoods, demanding that foreigners leave and accusing them of taking jobs and housing from South Africans.

Humanitarian groups and local authorities said the attacks have created an urgent crisis. Families have taken shelter in police stations, churches, community halls and temporary camps, often with little more than the clothes they were wearing when they fled. Aid workers warned that displaced people need food, blankets, medical care and protection, and that women, children and asylum seekers are especially vulnerable.

The violence has also disrupted already fragile communities. Small businesses owned by foreign nationals have been looted or burned, depriving families of their livelihoods and leaving neighborhoods without shops that many residents rely on for basic goods. Some migrants said they feared returning home even if the immediate violence subsided, while others said they were considering leaving South Africa altogether.

Officials and analysts said the unrest reflects a volatile mix of social and economic pressures. South Africa has one of the continent’s largest economies, but millions of people continue to live in poverty, particularly in townships and informal settlements where unemployment is high and public services are stretched. Competition for low-paid work, housing and government assistance has fueled resentment, with foreigners often blamed for hardships rooted in broader inequality and failures in service delivery.

At the same time, civic leaders and rights groups said xenophobic rhetoric and weak protection for migrants have helped create an atmosphere in which foreigners can be scapegoated. They warned that unless the government addresses both the immediate security threat and the underlying social conditions, similar outbreaks could recur.

President Thabo Mbeki condemned the attacks, calling on South Africans to reject xenophobia and violence against fellow Africans. He said the assaults were a betrayal of the country’s values and its history of receiving support from neighboring countries during the anti-apartheid struggle. Mbeki urged communities to stop the attacks and said law enforcement agencies would act against those responsible.

Government officials said additional police units were being sent to affected areas and that emergency relief was being coordinated for displaced residents. But in several communities, fear remained high as rumors of further attacks spread and foreigners stayed away from their homes.
